title: Semantic Search
shortDefinition: A search technique that finds content based on conceptual meaning rather than exact keyword matches.
definition: Semantic search is a search technique that finds content based on conceptual meaning rather than exact keyword matching — surfacing relevant results even when the query uses different words than the source content, by comparing the underlying meaning rather than literal text overlap. Semantic search powers modern enterprise search, ecommerce product discovery, and is the retrieval foundation underlying RAG systems.

sections.title: How semantic search works
sections.description: Semantic search converts both queries and content into embeddings for meaning-based comparison.

content.text: Semantic search converts both the search query and the searchable content into embeddings — numerical representations capturing meaning — then finds content whose embeddings are mathematically closest to the query's embedding. This allows a search for 'reduce employee turnover' to surface a document about 'improving staff retention,' something exact keyword matching would miss entirely since the words don't overlap, even though the concepts are nearly identical.

items: Embeddings — numerical representations capturing meaning.
Query embedding — convert the user's search question.
Content embeddings — convert all searchable content.
Similarity search — find content with closest embeddings.
Conceptual matching — surfacing meaning, not just words.

content.title: The key insight
content.text: Semantic search finds meaning, not just words — 'reduce employee turnover' finds 'improving staff retention' even though no words overlap.

Pure semantic search excels at conceptual matching but can sometimes underperform on queries where exact term matching matters — searching for a specific product SKU, an exact legal citation, or a precise technical term where you want the literal match, not a conceptually 'similar' result. Hybrid search combines semantic similarity with traditional keyword matching, capturing the strengths of both approaches — most production enterprise and ecommerce search systems use hybrid search rather than semantic search alone, for this reason.

sections.title: Limitations and risks of semantic search

content.text: Semantic search has limitations. It can miss exact term matches without hybrid search, and embedding models may not capture domain-specific nuances without tuning. Vector database infrastructure adds operational complexity, and relevance can degrade if embedding models aren't updated. Semantic search also requires significant content to work well — sparse content with limited embedding coverage may yield poor results, and the conceptual matching can sometimes surface irrelevant results that keyword search would avoid.

items: Exact term weakness — may miss precise matches without hybrid search.
Domain tuning needed — embedding models may not capture domain nuances.
Infrastructure complexity — vector databases add operational overhead.
Relevance degradation — quality can decay without model updates.
Content dependency — sparse content yields poor results.
Irrelevant results — can surface conceptually similar but contextually wrong results.
Cost — embedding generation and vector search add compute costs.

content.title: Important
content.text: Semantic search is powerful but not a complete replacement for keyword search in most production systems — hybrid search is typically the right approach.

faqs.title: Frequently asked questions about semantic search

items.question: What's the difference between semantic search and keyword search?
items.answer: Keyword search matches exact words or phrases; semantic search finds conceptually related content even when the wording differs, by comparing meaning rather than literal text.

items.question: Should we use pure semantic search or hybrid search?
items.answer: Most production systems benefit from hybrid search, combining semantic matching's conceptual strength with keyword matching's precision for exact terms; ClickMasters recommends the right balance based on your specific query patterns.

items.question: Can semantic search work across multiple languages?
items.answer: Yes, with appropriate multilingual embedding models; ClickMasters scopes language requirements during Discovery.

items.question: How do you measure whether semantic search is actually better than our current search?
items.answer: ClickMasters validates search relevance against your specific query patterns and content, giving you a measured comparison rather than relying on a general claim about semantic search superiority.

items.question: How long does a semantic search project take?
items.answer: 8–22 weeks depending on content volume and whether hybrid search or multi-source search is required.

items.question: Is semantic search the same technology underlying RAG?
items.answer: Yes, RAG's retrieval step typically uses semantic search (via embeddings and a vector database) to find relevant content before generating an answer — semantic search is a core building block of RAG.

items.question: What are common embedding models for semantic search?
items.answer: Common models include OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small/large, Cohere's embed models, Sentence-BERT, and E5. The right choice depends on your content type, language, and performance requirements.

items.question: How do you handle new content in semantic search?
items.answer: New content must be embedded and indexed in the vector database. ClickMasters builds ingestion pipelines that automatically generate embeddings and update the search index as content is added or changed.

items.question: What is hybrid search and when should I use it?
items.answer: Hybrid search combines semantic (vector) search with keyword (lexical) search. It's the recommended approach for production systems where users need both conceptual discovery and exact match capabilities.

items.question: How does semantic search handle stop words and common terms?
items.answer: Unlike keyword search, semantic search is less affected by stop words (like 'the', 'a') because embeddings capture meaning from the overall context rather than individual term importance. This is one advantage over traditional keyword search.
